items.title: How City Crows and Country Crows See the World Differently
items.author: Devin Reese
items.summary: What scares them is generally defined by where they’re from The post How City Crows and Country Crows See the World Differently appeared first on Nautilus .

images.caption: Lámina de Nautilus
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente

items.cleanReaderHtml:
What scares them is generally defined by where they’re from

We humans typically hesitate upon encountering new things. Whether it’s a food we’ve never heard of before or an odd-looking object in the middle of the road, it’s natural to take a moment to ascertain if something is an opportunity or a threat. In a recent study published in the journal Behavioral Ecology , biologists Dave J. Colucci and Anne Clark of Binghamton University documented that crows have such “neophobia too.” In fact, their upbringings shape which stuff triggers hesitation in them.

Colucci and Clark compared the reactions of American crows ( Corvus brachyrhynchos ) from the city and the countryside to novel objects. The city crows lived in Ithaca, New York, which by crow standards is urban, while the country crows lived in Dryden, a nearby rural area. Ten families of crows at each site were selected for experiments that were conducted on their respective home turfs.

First, the crows were fed peanuts in the shell, a preferred food no matter where a crow is from. Then, once they got used to the presence of humans, the crows were offered a series of objects alongside the familiar peanuts: a rock, an ear of corn, a takeout food container, and a wooden lamp base (definitely not your standard control object).

You’d think that country crows might be more wary in general, given the less humanized environments they inhabit, but it was actually the urban crows that showed more neophobia. “You can think of it as a blunt, anti-predator strategy in rural areas. Don’t take any chances, don’t stop to assess; let’s just be safe,” said Clark in a press release .

For each group, though, the familiar objects caused less hesitation than the novel ones. For the city crows, the takeout container wasn’t puzzling, while the country crows showed no wariness with the corn. The lamp base, well, that was jarring for both of them.

The researchers also gauged the crows’ fear of humans by seeing how they responded to eye contact. For city crows, a person staring directly at them was more likely to send them fleeing than a person looking away. Meanwhile, the more human-naïve country crows flew off whenever someone got too close, regardless of where the person was looking.

Those country bumpkins just aren’t used to the hustle and bustle of big city life.

Devin Reese is the executive editor of Natural History and a science writer based in Alexandria, Virginia.

Not the most aesthetically pleasing look, but essential for survival

A team of biologists sent people on a safari of their own homes

items.title: Naufragio en Ibiza: ¿cómo pudo hundirse un buque moderno como el Med Emre, sin un gran temporal?
items.author: Bismarck Jigena Antelo, Profesor Titular de Universidad de Cádiz, Area de Cienci
items.summary: Un buque de apenas siete años de antigüedad, dotado de doble casco y navegando por el Mediterráneo, acaba de hundirse cerca de Ibiza. ¿Era especialmente adverso el estado de la mar? ¿Qué podemos averiguar a partir de su trayectoria?

images.caption: Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen extraída de la fuente original
The Conversation

videos.caption: The Conversation

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Un buque de apenas siete años de antigüedad, dotado de doble casco y navegando por el Mediterráneo, acaba de hundirse cerca de Ibiza. El Med Emre tenía 120 metros de eslora y llevaba bandera de Malta. Había salido de Algeciras el martes 24 de noviembre con destino a Barcelona y transportaba unas 7 000 toneladas de gasóleo. Uno de sus 17 tripulantes ha fallecido, y 6 se encuentran heridos.

Las primeras informaciones apuntan a una vía de agua. Pero una vía de agua explica cómo comienza una inundación, no necesariamente por qué se produce.

¿Era especialmente adverso el estado de la mar? ¿Qué podemos averiguar a partir de la trayectoria del buque? Los registros de navegación y las mediciones de oleaje ofrecen algunas pistas, aunque todavía quedan muchas preguntas por responder.

Siete mil toneladas de gasóleo

En la madrugada del jueves 26, Salvamento Marítimo movilizó tres helicópteros y varias embarcaciones para rescatar a sus tripulantes. Las autoridades activaron también el plan de contingencias por contaminación marítima.

Las primeras noticias hablaban de 1,2 millones de litros de crudo. Sin embargo, ni el producto ni la cantidad eran correctos. El buque transportaba gasóleo, cuya densidad es aproximadamente un 16 % inferior a la del agua. Por tanto, 7 000 toneladas equivalen a unos 8,3 millones de litros. Casi siete veces la cifra inicialmente difundida.

La diferencia no es menor. Tanto el volumen como las características del hidrocarburo condicionan las actuaciones frente a un posible vertido.

A diferencia del fuelóleo pesado que transportaba el Prestige, el gasóleo se evapora y dispersa con mayor rapidez. Sin embargo, también puede producir efectos tóxicos importantes sobre los organismos marinos.

También conviene recordar que la cantidad transportada no equivale necesariamente a la cantidad vertida.

Las pistas confusas en su trayectoria

Actualmente, los grandes buques mercantes disponen de un sistema de identificación automática, conocido como AIS por sus siglas en inglés. Este sistema transmite periódicamente información sobre su posición, velocidad y dirección de desplazamiento.

Su análisis permite reconstruir buena parte de la trayectoria del Med Emre durante las horas anteriores al accidente. Así, sabemos que navegaba aparentemente con normalidad durante la tarde del miércoles. Se dirigía hacia Barcelona a una velocidad de unos 11 nudos (unos 21 kilómetros por hora).

Sin embargo, algo cambió bruscamente aquella noche. En apenas cinco minutos, entre las 22:22 y las 22:27, su velocidad pasó de 10,3 a 4,5 nudos. Simultáneamente, su dirección de desplazamiento cambió unos 120 grados.

Durante la siguiente hora y media, el buque se desplazó lentamente hacia el este-sureste, aproximadamente en la dirección hacia la que soplaba el viento.

A las 23:58 dejó de transmitir su posición.

Este comportamiento resulta compatible con una pérdida de propulsión y una posterior deriva. También podría reflejar una maniobra de emergencia seguida de dificultades para mantener el control del buque. Los datos no permiten determinar cuál de estas circunstancias se produjo. Pero sí ayudan a identificar el momento en que la navegación dejó de ser normal.

¿Era el estado de la mar excepcional?

Cuando se produce un naufragio, una de las primeras explicaciones que suelen considerarse es la existencia de un fuerte temporal, más cuando ese día la Agencia Estatal de Meteorología había activado un aviso amarillo por vientos del oeste y olas de hasta tres metros.

Para conocer mejor las condiciones marítimas, hemos analizado los registros de dos boyas de Puertos del Estado, estaciones flotantes fondeadas en el mar que miden en tiempo real variables oceanográficas y meteorológicas, como el oleaje, el viento, las corrientes y la temperatura del agua. Una está situada frente a Valencia, al oeste del accidente. La otra, cerca de la isla de Dragonera, al este. A las diez de la noche, poco antes del cambio de trayectoria del buque, la altura significante del oleaje era de 1,4 metros en Valencia y de 2,5 metros en Dragonera.

La altura significante representa aproximadamente la media del tercio de las olas más altas. Esto significa que algunas olas pueden superar considerablemente ese valor. De hecho, las mayores olas registradas durante el intervalo de medición alcanzaron los 2,2 y 4,3 metros, respectivamente.

Aunque estas condiciones pueden resultar incómodas para la navegación, no parecen extraordinarias para un mercante de 120 metros de eslora. No obstante, las boyas no estaban situadas en el punto exacto del accidente, por lo que no conocemos la altura ni la dirección de las olas que incidieron directamente sobre el buque.

¿Cómo puede hundirse un buque de doble casco?

El doble casco constituye una importante medida de seguridad frente a accidentes y vertidos de hidrocarburos. Podemos imaginarlo como dos envolturas metálicas separadas por un espacio intermedio. Si se perfora la exterior, la interior puede impedir que el agua alcance la carga.

Sin embargo, esta protección no hace que un buque sea insumergible. Una avería en una tubería que comunica con el mar, por ejemplo, puede provocar la inundación de la cámara de máquinas. Si el agua alcanza los motores o los generadores eléctricos, el buque puede perder su capacidad de maniobra. Además, el agua acumulada en el interior puede reducir su estabilidad. Si la inundación progresa hacia otros compartimentos, la situación se agravaría rápidamente.

Pero podrían existir otras posibles causas, como daños estructurales, fallos en elementos de cierre o problemas relacionados con la distribución de la carga.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The latest species discovery from a team at the Field Museum in Chicago takes us way back: more than 300 million years back, in fact.

This is long before dinosaurs roamed the Earth, in the late Carboniferous period, when the area around what is now Chicago would have been a swampy river delta. Imagine giant insects buzzing through the air, huge millipedes slithering along the ground, and strange amphibians splitting their time between land and water.

Read more: “ How “Useless” Science Unraveled an Amphibian Apocalypse ”

The newly identified species, recorded in a study published in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology , fits into that amphibian category. It’s called Jeanerpeton mazonensis , and it came to light after a thorough analysis of a fossil found in 1965 at the well-known Mazon Creek site in Illinois.

With its narrow snout, toe pads, and distinctive bone structure, the creature becomes one of the oldest relatives of modern-day frogs and salamanders that we know about—and a crucial new data point on the evolutionary chart.

Two of the researchers who made the discovery, Allison Sefcovic and Payton Kohlberg, were involved as part of the Women in Science Intern program at the Field Museum. The name of the species is a tribute to their mothers—both named Jean—and translates as “Jean’s crawler from Mazon Creek.”

The early amphibian was previously identified as being a member of the more common Amphibamus grandiceps species. The researchers pulled it from a “waste bin taxon,” a sort of dumping ground where similar species are lumped together until there’s enough time to study them properly.

High-resolution photography and CT scanning techniques were used to reconstruct what J. mazonensis would have looked like, and the characteristics (particularly around the nose and teeth) that make it distinct from other species—and indeed establish a whole new genus.

David Nield has written about science and technology for more than 20 years. His work has appeared in a wide range of publications, including Wired, Popular Science, The Guardian , and Gizmodo .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Photographs by Edward Burtynsky show us how climate-change art can light a path out of despair

COAL TRAIN: Coal Train Near Gillette, Wyoming, USA, 2015, pictures the everyday reality of the Powder River Basin, among the most productive coal deposits in the United States. Everything seems just fine—yet we know it’s not.

In the middle of October a few years ago, I was hit by a crisis of anxiety and despair. There had been a death in the family, I was unhappy at work, and I was confronting the existential doubt of middle age.

But above all, it was the global political and environmental situation that really made me panic. Fires, floods, hurricanes, heat waves—these were clearly getting more severe and more common all the time. The nations of the world had already met in Paris and agreed to limit global warming to no more than 2 degrees C above preindustrial levels, but that pact was looking unrealizable. Economies all over the world were prioritizing business as usual, even a growing nationalism, over the promised transformations. I was hopeless—I felt the planet was doomed and there was nothing I could do.

This story is from “The Hot Issue,” the latest from Nautilus . To get it in print, join by Nov 30 .

I began to heal, in the following winter, spring, and summer, largely through practices of connection: connecting to other people, to my work, to nature, and to a sense of purpose. Key to all of these was a connection to art—to its powers of expressing sadness, disappointment, and criticism, on the one hand, and of promoting feelings of innovation, joy, and meaning, on the other. Visiting exhibitions, teaching about art, and even making my own photographs gave me a sense of collective belonging and helped me to see a path for my own modest contribution to our gigantic world.

As we now know too well, rising concentrations of CO 2 and other greenhouse gasses have raised the average temperature on Earth well over 1 degree C warmer than before industrialization, hotter than at any time in the entire history of Homo sapiens . The results of the heat include desertification, rising seas, more extreme storms, and worsening wildfires. Humans and other beings are confronted with water shortage, food scarcity, dehydration, trauma, and death. Even on days we do not suffer directly, we often feel fear and sadness.

Unquestionably, solving the climate crisis will require technical and political solutions. But it will also require a remaking of some of the foundational beliefs of contemporary global civilization. We cannot build 21st-century civilization on unsustainable ideas and values carried over from the Enlightenment and industrial modernity. That’s where the powers of art come in.

We can turn to art for the ways in which its creativity and innovation can help ignite the process of remaking our structures of thought. Art can be a guide toward connection, well-being, action, and balance. It can help us reconceive our world. It can push us to unlearn the philosophies, myths, and fantasies that got us into this global existential crisis.

A reasonable person might argue that art is just entertainment, a distraction from what really matters. But art is different from everything else we see and think about every day. Most of the time we are consumed with short-term productivity. We have projects to finish at work, laundry to do, and loved ones to care for. We make calculations, in short, to achieve our immediate goals.

This is largely how it should be: A productive mindset allows us to survive and succeed. Art, however—as the philosopher Immanuel Kant argued centuries ago—is wonderfully purposeless. It is a key realm of human activity that exists not as a tool but instead for its own, illogical sake. And yet this very purposelessness allows art to be a great source of reorientation, growth, and learning.

Art offers us intimacy, creativity, connection, and critical engagement with our values. It puts us in contact with the deeper things we necessarily sideline in the everyday. It invites empathetic understanding of other human beings, and of plants and animals. Art involves critique but also wonder and love. It taps into the transformative power of emotion. Art provokes us, promoting radical dreams beyond our normal trains of thought. Art insists that things could be different. It helps us flex the muscle of imagining a reality other than the one we now occupy.

One of the great compounding difficulties of the climate crisis is that we—I mean all of us human beings here on Earth, suffering acutely or subconsciously—do not grasp it. We see photographs of a devastating flood, hear stories from a friend whose house went up, so fast, in flames. But we still have almost no tools for connecting these traumas to our everyday experience: our work, our shopping, our relationships, our going out at night for fun. As a result, we too often feel disconnected—from the crisis, from each other, even from our own grief and hope.

In part, the problem is that climate change is so devilishly difficult to visualize. Our conundrum is like that of the proverbial blind men apprehending the elephant: We can perceive this effect or that one (California’s fire, Pakistan’s flood), but the whole remains almost impossibly abstract.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
As long as humans have been around, we’ve been curious about existential questions like, Why are we here? And how do things work? That goes for our own bodies, too. But in our era of modern science and medicine, it’s difficult to imagine a time when physicians weren’t familiar with all of the bones in the skeleton, how a baby grows inside a womb, or how the cardiovascular system works. Even the profession that comes to mind when we think of a doctor didn’t really emerge until the past few centuries. During the medieval period, barber-surgeons were the primary medical practitioners (yes, the people who cut hair also conducted surgeries).

As medicine morphed into a scientific and intellectual pursuit, academies cropped up starting in the late 1700s, such as the College of Philadelphia—the first medical school in the U.S.—and the Edinburgh School of Surgery in Scotland. Ethics were, let’s say, malleable. In Edinburgh, a legal shortage of fresh cadavers used for study in the early 1800s spawned a shady underground trade in bodies, many of which were dug up from new burials in the dead of night. And then there were the famous serial murders committed by William Burke and William Hare, who cashed in by selling well over a dozen of their victims’ corpses to anatomist Robert Knox for use during his lectures. Suffice it to say, some scholars really wanted to understand our innards.

Slated for release in January, The Book of the Human Body delves into the art and science of anatomy, disease, reproduction, and more. Published by TASCHEN, the two-volume set compiles more than 950 images from over 75 rare books and manuscripts from around the world. From ancient analyses to medieval studies to modern diagrams, the anthology surveys the breadth of eras and cultural influences that have shaped our understanding of our physical selves.

Authored by medical historian Richard Barnett, the book celebrates universality and unquenched curiosity. Despite sleeping, breathing, and walking around in our bodies every day, we are often still mystified by much of what makes them work. Throughout history, that sense of wonder has remained constant. Barnett says, “Whatever they might represent, whatever they might express, these extraordinary images have lost none of their power to shock or captivate, to teach or inspire.”

Illustrations include a silk manuscript dated to 168 B.C.E., discovered in a tomb in southern China, which features 44 figures engaged in exercises of “self-cultivation,” plus excerpts from Andreas Vesalius’s anatomical atlas, Fabrica, published in 1543. “In all of these examples, the illustrations stand out not only as objects of medical understanding, but as conspicuous works of art in their own right,” the publisher says.

Pre-order your copy on Bookshop.

items.title: Del Prestige a Ibiza, ¿qué protección ofrece hoy un petrolero de doble casco?
items.author: José Ygnacio Pastor Caño, Catedrático de Universidad en Ciencia e Ingeniería de
items.summary: El Med Emre volcó frente a Ibiza con unas 7.000 toneladas de combustible. ¿Cómo puede un petrolero volcado panza arriba seguir desplazándose y, sobre todo, conservar su carga?

The Conversation

videos.caption: The Conversation

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A las 9:26 del 26 de noviembre de 2026, el barco que se daba por hundido mostró la quilla, boca abajo. Un avión de Salvamento Marítimo localizó al Med Emre, todavía a flote, a unos 35 kilómetros al noroeste de Ibiza. La noche anterior había pedido auxilio en su travesía de Algeciras a Barcelona. De sus diecisiete tripulantes, uno murió. ¿Seguía a bordo su carga, unas 7 000 toneladas de combustible??

Imaginemos que leemos la noticia mientras desayunamos en un bar. En una servilleta dibujamos el petrolero en sección, como si le hubiéramos cortado una rebanada. Dejamos la quilla hacia arriba y vemos cómo la camarera, con esa delicadeza que merecemos los despistados, le da media vuelta al papel. Le agradecemos el gesto y, con la misma cortesía, le damos otra media vuelta. ¿Quién ha puesto el barco del derecho, la camarera o nosotros?

¿Se puede flotar al revés?

Mientras se enfría el café, imaginemos una prueba que podemos hacer luego en casa. Pegamos un poco de plastilina a un costado de una botella de plástico vacía y bien cerrada. La tumbamos en el agua del fregadero, la giramos hasta dejar el pegote a un lado y la soltamos. La botella rueda hasta que el lastre queda abajo. Ha girado sin dejar de flotar ni perder un gramo. El agua empuja hacia arriba y la gravedad tira hacia abajo. La botella gira cuando el peso y el empuje actúan a lo largo de dos ejes verticales distintos.

Hace más de dos mil años, Arquímedes explicó que el empuje equivale al peso del agua desplazada. Cuando un barco flota en equilibrio, esa agua pesa exactamente lo mismo que el barco. Si, tras volcar, quedan compartimentos estancos, un buque puede seguir desplazando suficiente agua incluso con la cubierta hacia el fondo. Así, averiguar cómo llegó el Med Emre a esa posición exige reconstruir la avería.

Volvamos a la servilleta. En la zona de carga, tracemos una segunda línea por dentro de los costados y del fondo, dejando un hueco entre ambas. Ya hemos dibujado el doble casco. Ahí cabe agua de lastre, y también una abolladura. Si en un accidente se abre la chapa exterior, el mar puede inundar ese hueco mientras la pared interior mantiene la carga. Si el daño atraviesa ambas paredes, el combustible puede escapar. El Med Emre dispone, además, de doce tanques de carga. Así, una brecha en uno de ellos puede dejar a salvo los once restantes.

¿Y qué cabe en el grosor de una capa del casco? Mucha ciencia, física e ingeniería de los materiales. A la chapa del casco de un barco le pedimos ductilidad, para que se abolle sin desgarrarse, y tenacidad de fractura, para que resista el avance de una grieta. En la acería, controlar el laminado y el enfriamiento permite afinar los granos –esos diminutos cristales que forman el acero– y mejorar su tenacidad.

Lo que se quedó dentro

Recordamos al Prestige por lo que perdió. Aquel petrolero de casco único se partió en dos frente a Galicia el 19 de noviembre de 2002. En total vertió unas 63 000 toneladas de fuel pesado. ¿Cuánto se pudo recuperar Dos años después se extrajeron por gravedad 13 800 toneladas de fuel del pecio, hundido a casi cuatro kilómetros de profundidad.

¿Y qué sabemos del Med Emre? La tarde del 26 de noviembre, Capitanía Marítima de Valencia informó de una pequeña mancha oleosa. La atribuyó provisionalmente a residuos del buque y consideró que los tanques de carga seguían intactos.

En este caso, el gasóleo que llevaba se evapora y se dispersa antes que el fuel pesado del Prestige, aunque también puede intoxicar a la fauna y flora marina.

En definitiva, para saber qué pasó en el Med Emre, y por qué, habrá que inspeccionar los daños. Y, si los hubiera, también habrá que intentar solucionar, una vez más, las consecuencias de sus vertidos en los ecosistemas marinos.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Our 2027 Innovators Under 35 competition is now open

Every year, MIT Technology Review honors 35 of the world’s brightest young scientists, entrepreneurs, and inventors in our Innovators Under 35 list. And starting today, our 2027 competition is officially open for nominations.

We’re on the hunt for researchers and founders who are engineering solutions to society’s most formidable problems, from human disease to climate change. We also recognize those who have made clever and useful inventions, important new scientific discoveries, or technological breakthroughs early in their careers.

Nominees can be based anywhere in the world, but must be under 35 on October 1, 2027. Have someone in mind? Or think you’d be a great candidate and want to put yourself forward? Here’s how to make a nomination for our 2027 list.

How cutting-edge prosthetics can help probe the human mind

There are a lot of remarkable things about Avi Davidson. A horrific injury as a teenager left him paralyzed and without a left hand. Today, his experience informs his work as a trauma therapist. He’s also taking part in a clinical trial of new tech that allows him to move—and feel with—a prosthetic hand.

Before the trial started, researchers scanned his brain to see how his missing left hand was represented in his brain. Will that change? And what might that mean for people who are born without limbs?

Here’s what a bionic hand might reveal about the mind.

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Nvidia’s crackdown on China’s chip access is reshaping Asian AI
 It just stopped server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries. (FT $)
+ Singapore is lobbying the US to keep its AI chip access. (Bloomberg $)
+ Asian economies have become increasingly dependent on Nvidia. (BBC)
+ But Chinese chip stocks have soared to their best day ever. (CNBC)
+ And AI-linked exports are still booming across Asia—for now. (WSJ $)
+ What’s next for Chinese open-source AI? (MIT Technology Review)

2 Hackers have breached the US Air Force’s flagship cloud platform
It holds sensitive tactical, personnel, and logistics data. (Reuters $)
+ A separate hack stole data from FIFA. (Guardian)
+ Another cyber attack has hit the UK’s pension and benefits systems. (BBC)

3 AI shopping bots have begun a $1 trillion holiday season test
Google, Amazon, Meta, and OpenAI are vying to reshape shopping. (Bloomberg $)
+ Many shoppers are turning to AI to find Black Friday deals. (Reuters $)
+ Retailers have called for new guardrails. (Guardian)

4 Cheap armed drones are terrorizing civilians around the world
Drone attacks rose 4,000% globally between 2020 and 2024. (ABC)
+ Europe has a drone-filled vision for future wars. (MIT Technology Review)

5 AI may soon break the internet’s encryption
New algorithms could crack public-key cryptography. (Nature)
+ The agentic web is here. (MIT Technology Review)

6 An experiment with ultracold atoms could unravel a quantum mystery
Physicists aim to reveal how long particles take to travel. (New Scientist $)

7 New images reveal the damage from NASA’s asteroid-deflection test
The crater from the Hera mission is the size of a stadium. (Gizmodo)
+ How close did Earth come to an asteroid impact? (MIT Technology Review)

8 Scientists have used GTA to model the effects of climate change
The game’s maps can simulate the effects of rising sea levels. (Wired $) 

9 X has added parental controls for teenagers
But it’s giving teens a say in the matter. (TechCrunch)

10 Jensen Huang is back—and so is his Denny’s plaque
The chain has restored the tribute to Nvidia’s supposed birthplace. (NYT $)

“I cannot check the tears from pouring on my coat.”

—Yu Kai, CEO of Chinese chip designer Horizon Robotics, quotes eighth-century poet Du Fu to the Financial Times to express his delight at Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia as “Jensanity” sweeps across both sides of the Taiwan Strait.


The curious case of the disappearing Lamborghinis

A new wave of theft is rocking the luxury car industry—mixing high-tech with old-school chop-shop techniques to snag vehicles while they’re in transit.

MIT Technology Review identified more than a dozen cases involving high-end vehicles, obtained court records, and spoke to law enforcement, brokers, drivers, and victims in multiple states to reveal how transport fraud is wreaking havoc across the country.

Find out how a new wave of transport fraud is wreaking havoc across the country.

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

+ A Japanese grandfather has turned his two cats into beloved photo models.
+ Why does “We Are the Champions” sound so stirring? A music theorist breaks it down.
+ Formula 1 champion Max Verstappen showed his incredible driving skills in a race against 100 amateur karters.
+ Take a tour of the world’s first Godzilla museum, which includes a life-size model of the monster that’s 120 meters long.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Earth is home to plenty of animals whose lifespans dwarf our own, and a lot of them seem to live in water. Now we can add one more to the list. According to a new study published in Communications Biology , the blue sucker—a bony, bottom-dwelling freshwater fish—can live up to 130 years.

A team of ichthyologists made the discovery after studying rock-like structures in the blue sucker’s inner ear called otoliths. These tiny calcium carbonate pebbles accumulate over the lifetime of the fish, like tree rings, which means if you carefully slice them open and count the layers, you can determine its age.

Read more: “ When Fake Nuclear Disaster Fallout Reached Los Angeles ”

After counting roughly 130 layers, the team was confident they’d identified the newest member of the centenarian fish club. But they had to be sure. After all, previous estimates of the blue sucker’s lifespan hovered around only 40 years. “When age estimates are that much older than previously thought, an additional line of evidence is needed to rigorously test their validity,” study author Alec Lackmann of the University of Minnesota Duluth explained in a statement .

So naturally they turned to atomic weaponry (or rather the effects of it). During the 1950s and 1960s, there were a lot of unregulated tests of nuclear bombs, which led to a global surge of atmospheric radioactive carbon-14 isotopes called the bomb pulse. Over the following decades, nation states gradually decided to stop testing, causing levels to steadily fall. Living things, being primarily made of carbon, showed the same pulse and decline in their carbon-14 levels over time. Testing blue sucker fish otoliths for carbon-14 revealed they lived through the same tumultuous period.

“To put a timeline on some of those older fish: the oldest one hatched around two years after Montana became a state, around the dawn of the automobile, like 20 years before the Titanic sank—it’s just wild,” study author Luke Holmquist with Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks said. “We start putting it in the context of what the landscape looked like when these fish hatched, and all the changes that have happened since—and they just keep swimming along in the river.”

It’s a remarkable finding, especially considering the blue sucker doesn’t just float along the bottom of lakes, preferring a faster-paced river lifestyle. And this new addition isn’t the only long-lived member of the sucker family. The bigmouth buffalo, smallmouth buffalo, and black buffalo (suckers, all) can each live over 100 years. In fact, according to Lackmann’s previous research , these buffalofish actually improve with age. Compared to youngsters, buffalofish in their 80s and 90s showed improved immune function and better stress responses.

Unfortunately, the blue sucker may not be faring as well. Of the 23 states the fish is native to, it’s categorized as imperiled in 22 of them. In Montana, population studies have turned up virtually no smaller (i.e., young) specimens, possibly due to habitat fragmentation caused by dam construction.

It’s likely there are fish alive today who had to adapt, which makes their longevity all the more impressive.

What scares them is generally defined by where they’re from

Not the most aesthetically pleasing look, but essential for survival

items.title: ¿Por qué escuchar la palabra ‘calladita’ activa todos los resortes?
items.author: Olga Cruz Moya, Profesora titular de universidad, área de Lengua española, Unive
items.summary: Una sola palabra, ‘calladita’, encendió el último debate electoral a cuatro en España. Más allá de la intención de quien la pronunció, el diminutivo activa una tradición que asocia el silencio femenino con la virtud y la belleza.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
El jueves 26 de noviembre, a tres días de las elecciones generales en España, el debate a cuatro de RTVE dejó una frase que ha eclipsado buena parte de las propuestas. Ada Colau (Frente Amplio) reprochaba a Alberto Núñez Feijóo (PP) la gestión de la dana de 2024, y este respondió: “Buena gestión es ponerse al frente de una emergencia nacional y no salir huyendo de Paiporta, y usted, calladita”.

Pedro Sánchez intervino de inmediato: “¿Pero qué machismo es ese?”. Colau replicó que no pensaba quedarse “calladita”. Feijóo explicó después que había omitido el verbo (“y usted estuvo calladita”), es decir, que reprochaba a Colau su silencio ante la actuación del presidente; su partido difundió por escrito la versión con “estaba calladita” y él mismo retiró la expresión “si ha molestado a alguien”. Al día siguiente, insistió en que Sumar y Frente Amplio habían estado “calladitos y calladitas” ante la corrupción.

¿Por qué una sola palabra provoca una reacción tan grande? La lingüística puede darnos algunas respuestas.

Dos lecturas para una misma palabra

La frase admite dos interpretaciones. En la primera, “calladita” es un predicativo con un verbo elidido: “usted estuvo calladita”, un reproche por no haber hablado. En la segunda, funciona como una fórmula directiva, casi un imperativo sin verbo, del tipo “¡calladita!”, que ordena silencio. La elipsis es habitual en la oralidad, pero aquí deja el enunciado abierto, y el oyente lo completa con lo que tiene más a mano: la entonación, el gesto de señalar y, sobre todo, un marco cultural muy reconocible, el de “calladita estás más guapa”.

Álvaro García Meseguer, pionero en el estudio del sexismo lingüístico en español, sostenía que la lengua como sistema no es sexista: el sexismo puede estar en quien habla o en quien escucha. El caso del debate ilustra bien esa idea. Aunque la intención fuera la primera lectura, la segunda está tan arraigada que se activa casi sola. Y lo que la activa es, precisamente, el diminutivo.

El diminutivo que no empequeñece

El sufijo -ito/-ita no sirve solo para hacer las cosas pequeñas. Con adjetivos y participios suele intensificar: subraya que un estado se ha alcanzado por completo. Calladita no es “un poco callada”, sino “completamente callada”, como “quietecito” o “cuidadito”. Pero el diminutivo tiene además un fuerte valor afectivo, y ese afecto tiene un destinatario prototípico: la infancia. “Quietecita” o “a dormir tempranito” son fórmulas que se dirigen, sobre todo, a niños y niñas.

Cuando ese registro se dirige a una mujer adulta, y además en un contexto de poder como un debate presidencial, se produce un desplazamiento: la interlocutora pasa simbólicamente al lugar de quien debe ser corregida con cariño.

La psicología social tiene un nombre para esta combinación de afecto y control. La teoría del sexismo ambivalente distingue entre un sexismo hostil y otro benevolente, que se expresa a través de un paternalismo protector. “Calladita estás más guapa” es casi un ejemplo de manual: ordena el silencio, pero lo envuelve en un piropo.

Leer más: Cuando la escuela enseñaba que ‘calladita estás más guapa’: los manuales de cortesía y la educación lingüística

Una tradición milenaria de silencio

La idea de que el silencio embellece a la mujer no nace en el refranero. La estudiosa del mundo clásico Mary Beard abre su ensayo Mujeres y poder con el primer canto de la Odisea, en el que Telémaco manda callar a Penélope y la devuelve a su telar porque la palabra pública es cosa de hombres.

La tradición cristiana consagró el “mulier taceat in ecclesia” paulino (es decir, “que la mujer calle en la iglesia”), y en el siglo XVI fray Luis de León escribía en La perfecta casada (1583) que “es justo que se precien de callar todas”, tanto las que saben como las que no.

El refrán actual es la versión popular y doméstica de ese ideal. Su origen exacto no es fácil de fechar, porque vive sobre todo en la oralidad: en los corpus de libros digitalizados apenas aparece, pero los archivos de folclore recogen testimonios de mujeres que lo oyeron de sus abuelas como un consejo. Circula a ambos lados del Atlántico, con variantes como “calladita te ves más bonita”, habitual en México y otros países de América.

La historiadora de la lengua Lola Pons acaba de dedicar a estos mandatos un ensayo, que recorre las formas en las que el español ha pedido, impuesto y roto el silencio, desde la Edad Media hasta las redes sociales. Pons se ocupa del silenciamiento de las mujeres: sitúa fórmulas como “calladita estás más guapa” en una tradición que alababa a la mujer callada y censuraba a la que hablaba demasiado, y recuerda que, incluso en parlamentos paritarios, las mujeres siguen disponiendo de menos tiempo de palabra que sus compañeros. Callar y hacer callar casi nunca son gestos ajenos a las relaciones de poder.

De hecho, una diputada mexicana a la que le cerraron el micrófono en 2025 denunció que la habían silenciado recordando que eso “es lo que siempre se ha hecho con nosotras”.

Del refrán a la pantalla y la canción

La fórmula ha pasado a la cultura popular, casi siempre para cuestionarla. La periodista Carme Chaparro la eligió como título de su ensayo feminista. La cantante Brisa Fenoy abre su canción “Bonita” con un diálogo en el que un hombre le espeta a su pareja que “calladita estás más bonita”, antes de que la letra desmonte la idea. Bad Bunny tituló “Callaíta” su canción sobre una chica aparentemente discreta.

En el cine, Miguel Faus llevó a la gran pantalla Calladita, sobre una empleada doméstica a la que se le exige invisibilidad y silencio, y en México se rodó el cortometraje de terror Calladita te ves más bonita.

¿Y ‘calladito estás más guapo’?

Existe, desde luego. Se dice a los niños, se dice en broma entre amigos, y el propio Feijóo recurrió al masculino al hablar de “calladitos y calladitas”. Pero no funciona igual.

Aquí resulta útil un concepto clásico de los estudios sobre sexismo y lengua: los duales aparentes, pares de palabras que cambian de significado o de connotación según se refieran a un hombre o a una mujer. En un artículo anterior en The Conversation analicé uno de los más conocidos, “zorro” y “zorra”: el masculino evoca astucia y el femenino, promiscuidad.

“Calladito” y “calladita” no son duales aparentes en el diccionario, porque significan lo mismo. Lo son en el uso: la forma es simétrica, pero la carga cultural no. El masculino es una ocurrencia puntual; el femenino arrastra un refrán, una moral y siglos de tratados que vinculan el silencio de las mujeres con su valor y su aspecto. Por eso, cuando un hombre manda callar a otro hombre, no suele recurrir al diminutivo ni a la belleza. Basta recordar el “¿Por qué no te callas?” que Juan Carlos I dirigió a Hugo Chávez en 2007: era una orden directa, sin cariño fingido ni alusión al físico.

No hace falta atribuir una intención machista a nadie para reconocer que ciertas palabras llegan cargadas de antemano. El diminutivo de “calladita” no es un rasgo neutro del sistema, sino un recurso que, dirigido a una mujer en un espacio de poder, la sitúa en un lugar infantil y evoca la vieja asociación entre silencio femenino y virtud. En un debate cuyo objetivo es precisamente disputarse la palabra, ningún diminutivo es pequeño.

items.author: David Colaço & Philipp Haueis
items.summary: We have an astonishing number of models of how the mind works. All of them neglect something essential - by David Colaço & Philipp Haueis Read on Aeon

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The Moment the Snow Melts (2025), an installation by the Japanese artist Chiharu Shiota, in Milan, Italy. Photo by Emanuele Cremaschi/Getty Images

is a historian and philosopher of science at the Munich Center for Mathematical Philosophy at LMU Munich, Germany.

is assistant professor at the Department of Philosophy, and a member of the Institute for Studies of Science at Bielefeld University, Germany.

Making sense of the mind is, in part, a matter of modelling, and philosophers and scientists have created an astonishing number of models. Some liken the mind to a computer. Some emphasise symbols and ‘mentalese’, a hypothesised ‘language of thought’. Some start from the brain and its physical, neural basis. These models aren’t necessarily in conflict: for instance, the ‘working memory’ model proposed by the psychologists Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch may complement ‘predictive processing’ models of vision or attention theorised by the computational neuroscientists Rajesh Rao, Dana Ballard and Karl Friston. The domain is crowded, and still growing.

However, nearly all of these models neglect something essential to how the human mind functions: metabolism. They describe what the mind computes, or how its neurons signal, but not the metabolic work by which the brain acquires energy, maintains homeostasis, and disposes of waste. Without taking metabolism into consideration, our models are in danger of becoming untethered from real-world constraints, turning the ancient goal of understanding the mind into a wild goose chase.

‘M etabolism’ refers to activities that all biological systems, the brain included, carry out in order to stay alive. It includes energy use, but also maintenance, regulation and waste removal. Metabolism informs models of how our muscles work when we run, how our lungs work when we breathe, and how our immune system works when we get sick. Since the human mind has something to do with the brain, it stands to reason that metabolism should inform models of how our brain works when we think. And, indeed, most scholars nowadays tend to accept that the brain is important to understanding the mind, even if they leave it out of their models.

The brain is a quirky organ, metabolically speaking. It consumes a lot of energy compared with other parts of the human body. Though it makes up around 2 per cent of an adult’s body mass, it consumes about 20 per cent of its calories. Yet it is impressively efficient. The brain on average operates at about 20 watts – less than an incandescent lightbulb. A ‘lightbulb moment’, in other words, probably consumes less energy than an actual lightbulb.

According to one study by William Levy and Victoria Calvert of the University of Virginia, the electrical signals (or ‘spikes’) that send information use only about 3.5 watts. Building and strengthening synapses, which is how information is stored, uses about 1.3 watts. It is not entirely understood how the brain can do so much with so little, but part of the answer is evolution: organisms with more efficient brains had a selective advantage for searching for food and avoiding predators. The human mind operates under tremendous metabolic constraints.

A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support

Focusing on metabolism might seem to fly in the face of much philosophical analysis of the mind. Many philosophers set the brain aside when building their theories, freeing the mind from its substratum. One reason is the widespread acceptance of multiple realisability, a view first set out by the philosopher Hilary Putnam in the 1960s, which holds that the same mental states can be realised by different neural states. What determines a mental state is what it does, not what it’s made of. This is how an octopus could still feel pain, even if its brain is unlike ours – it’s the state that matters, not the physical substratum. Some philosophers go further, adopting John Haugeland’s notion of ‘medium independence’: if mental states are computations – a mainstream view in cognitive science – then these states are independent of the specific medium in which they are embodied. Mental states are defined by formal rules, and these same rules can be implemented in different media. The familiar analogy is the computer : the same software (the mind) can be run on different hardware (the brain). Both views reject the idea that there is a one-to-one match between the mind and the brain. They suggest that the mind can be fruitfully studied on its own terms, making metabolism irrelevant to modelling.

Yet even brain-friendly philosophers have largely disregarded brain metabolism. Patricia Churchland, who urged philosophers to learn neuroscience, co-wrote a 1988 paper that defined the aim of computational neuroscience as explaining how the brain’s signals are used ‘to represent and process information’. But the chemistry that maintains those signals was lost in this framing. The philosopher Carl Craver and colleagues stay close to the biological ground when they argue that mechanisms are ‘entities and activities organised such that they are productive of regular changes’, for example neurotransmitters binding to receptors. But here too the energy that makes those activities possible figures as a background condition rather than as part of the explanation.

We argue that metabolism constrains which models of the mind are viable. But that does not require the mind to be uniquely realised by the brain: metabolic constraints narrow the options without settling on a single one. Consider the example of memory storage. It could occur via different brain processes, or in nonbiological media like silicon-based digital computers. Whatever the medium, all these systems will be constrained by energy use, maintenance and waste removal. A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support, and studying metabolism is how we find out where that limit lies.

S o the metabolic constraints on physical systems like brains cannot be ignored when modelling the mind. This means rethinking our stance towards views like multiple realisability and medium independence. Rather than taking them to be firm metaphysical commitments, we should think of them as working hypotheses: great starting points, but open to revision after new research.

Recently, the philosophers Mazviita Chirimuuta , Corey Maley and Rosa Cao have each argued that information-processing in brains depends on signal amplitudes, metabolic molecules and energy supply. This suggests a tight link between mind and metabolism, but it does not decisively rule out multiple realisability or medium independence. Instead, it shows that studying brain metabolism can test how much these hypotheses help us understand the mind. Looking at metabolism is therefore important, even if future science finds out that there is no one-to-one relation between mind and brain, that minds can exist in silicon, or that body and environment are essential for cognition.

35 Innovators under 35 2027 Call for Entries

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Every year, the editors at MIT Technology Review select 35 of the world’s top young scientists, entrepreneurs, and inventors to honor as our newest class of Innovators Under 35. And starting today, our 2027 competition is officially open for nominations.

We’re on the hunt for researchers and founders who are engineering solutions to some of the most formidable problems society faces, including human disease and climate change. We also recognize those who have made clever and useful inventions, important new scientific discoveries, or technological breakthroughs early in their careers.

We want to hear about people, based anywhere in the world, who are responsible for a major finding or advance and can show real-world impact from their work. To qualify for the list, a nominee must be under the age of 35 as of October 1, 2027 (that is, born on or after October 2, 1992).

Have someone in mind? Or think you’d be a great candidate and want to nominate yourself? Follow this link to suggest someone who you think should make our 2027 list. It’s free and takes only a few minutes. Just be sure to get your nomination in before the deadline—which is 11:59 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, January 19.

After the deadline, our editors will review all nominees and select a group of semifinalists, whom we’ll invite to complete a formal application. Then, dozens of expert judges will help us evaluate those applicants and settle on the finalists. You can read more about our selection process here.

We look forward to reviewing your nominations.

Imagen extraída de la fuente original

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Over the last few weeks, I’ve been talking to Alexander (Avi) Davidson. There are a lot of remarkable things about Avi. He sustained a horrific injury as a teenager, which left him paralyzed and without a left hand. Today, he uses his own experience to guide his practice as a trauma therapist.

He’s also taking part in a clinical trial of some new tech that allows him to move—and feel with—a prosthetic hand. Unlike standard prosthetics, this one connects directly to nerves in Avi’s arm. He literally has wires coming out of his arm to plug it in with.

Avi’s the ninth person to trial this tech. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently, for things like drinking from a cup (which is not easy) and writing (also not easy).

What struck me the most over our conversations was Avi’s outlook and approach to not just his injuries and learning to use this cutting-edge technology, but to life itself.

He has learned how to use something like seven different prosthetics in the 17 years since his accident. By taking part in this trial, he’s had to fit hundreds of hours of lab-based training and physical therapy around his demanding job. He had surgery to implant electrodes in his arm and will eventually need another to remove them. And he won’t even get to keep the latest prosthetic long term.

“While it’s unfortunate at times, and irritating at times, I do not regret what has come from [the accident], or the fact that it happened,” he told me. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”

The research team at the University of Utah that is running the trial hopes it will answer longstanding questions about the technology. How does it fare in a real-world setting, outside of the lab? What do people end up using it for? Where can improvements be made?

There may be some surprises along the way. Avi has found that his prosthetic wrist can feel sore and stiff when it’s been overused, just like his flesh-and-blood wrist. Weirdly, that feeling can be relieved by stretching it out. What’s going on here? No one really knows.

Scientists don’t know whether Avi’s brain will change as a result of using the bionic hand, either. Before the trial started, they performed brain scans to see how his missing left hand was represented in his brain. Will that change? And what might that mean for people who are born without limbs—how might a bionic limb affect their brains?

Avi will have the device until late January 2027 at the least, and potentially for another year. After that? Again, no one knows. It will depend on how the research is progressing, how Avi feels, and how much funding the team can secure. As a result, it’s not clear how long the device might even be expected to last in a person’s body.

I’ll be following this study, though, and will keep you posted.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
There aren’t many ways to experience the ancient world. We can learn its languages, at least the ones that have left behind decipherable writings; we can behold its artifacts; we can visit its ruins. But nothing gets us quite as close to entering the consciousness of our distant forebears as hearing the music — or at least the sounds — that they did. In the new Archaeologist’s Notebook video above, Giselle Király gives us a tour through ancient musical history, explaining the instruments of those times that survive in one form or another today. That tour begins at a much earlier point than many would expect: 40,000 years ago, in the depths of the last Ice Age, when humans were already punctuating their struggle for survival with organized sound.

As evidence, Király points to the “tiny, exquisitely crafted flutes carved from animal bone and mammoth ivory” discovered on cave floors around Europe. Surprisingly, when played in replica form, these vulture- or swan-bone flutes actually sound somewhat Middle Eastern. But whatever the stylistic traits of the music their original players produced, that music had the potential to confer benefits beyond immediate pleasure: “It would’ve connected people, built cohesion within the community,” and maybe even bridged “the land of the living with some spiritual world.” Each of the other discovered or reconstructed instruments, like swingable “bullroarers,” bone rasps, and lithophones (of the kind previously featured here on Open Culture) would have played its own sonic part to that end.

Király also discusses the lavishly decorated Lyres of Ur, the world’s oldest surviving stringed instruments; a 3,500-year-old Egyptian long-necked lute with a guitar-like fingerboard; and a set of 65 Chinese bianzhong bells covering a five-octave range. But music isn’t just about the objects it’s played with. Also important are the means of recording it, an ancient example of which Király cites in the Hurrian Hymn to Nikkal inscribed on a clay tablet around 1400 BC, the oldest known complete musical notation. Centuries later, in the Greek-speaking world — and in the more monumental form of a marble stele — a man named Seikilos recorded an epitaph to which we now refer by his name. The lyrics of this oldest completely preserved, fully playable musical composition exhort the listener: “While you live, shine. Have no grief at all.” For “life exists only for a short while,” and “time demands its toll.” The ancients needed to hear this no less, perhaps, than we do.

items.title: Vladimir Nabokov on What Makes a Good Reader
items.author: Maria Popova
items.summary: "A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader."

images.caption: Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Imagen extraída de la fuente original
The Marginalian

The Marginalian

items.cleanReaderHtml:
“A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader.”

“All attempts at gaining literary polish must begin with judicious reading,” H.P. Lovecraft advised aspiring writers. We’ve already seen that reading is a learned skill and an optimizable technique, and that non-reading is as important an intellectual choice as reading itself, so it follows that reading, more than the mere monolithic act of ingesting text, comes with degrees of mastery. But what, exactly, does it mean to be a good reader?

Vladimir Nabokov (April 22, 1899–July 2, 1977) was a man of wonderfully opinionated insights on literature and life. He was also, it turns out, equally opinionated in his criteria for what constitutes a good reader. In his collected Lectures on Literature (public library), Nabokov offers the following exercise, which he posed to students at a “remote provincial college” while on an extended lecture tour:

Select four answers to the question what should a reader be to be a good reader:

  1. The reader should belong to a book club.
  2. The reader should identify himself or herself with the hero or heroine.
  3. The reader should concentrate on the social-economic angle.
  4. The reader should prefer a story with action and dialogue to one with none.
  5. The reader should have seen the book in a movie.
  6. The reader should be a budding author.
  7. The reader should have imagination.
  8. The reader should have memory.
  9. The reader should have a dictionary.
  10. The reader should have some artistic sense.

The students leaned heavily on emotional identification, action, and the social-economic or historical angle. Of course, as you have guessed, the good reader is one who has imagination, memory, a dictionary, and some artistic sense–which sense I propose to develop in myself and in others whenever I have the chance.

He goes on to consider the element of time in reading, making a case for the value of rereading:

Incidentally, I use the word reader very loosely. Curiously enough, one cannot read a book: one can only reread it. A good reader, a major reader, an active and creative reader is a rereader. And I shall tell you why. When we read a book for the first time the very process of laboriously moving our eyes from left to right, line after line, page after page, this complicated physical work upon the book, the very process of learning in terms of space and time what the book is about, this stands between us and artistic appreciation. When we look at a painting we do not have to move our eyes in a special way even if, as in a book, the picture contains elements of depth and development. The element of time does not really enter in a first contact with a painting. In reading a book, we must have time to acquaint ourselves with it. We have no physical organ (as we have the eye in regard to a painting) that takes in the whole picture and then can enjoy its details. But at a second, or third, or fourth reading we do, in a sense, behave towards a book as we do towards a painting. However, let us not confuse the physical eye, that monstrous masterpiece of evolution, with the mind, an even more monstrous achievement. A book, no matter what it is—a work of fiction or a work of science (the boundary line between the two is not as clear as is generally believed)—a book of fiction appeals first of all to the mind. The mind, the brain, the top of the tingling spine, is, or should be, the only instrument used upon a book.

Complement with Mark Twain’s humorous list of the fourteen types of readers and Nabokov on the three qualities a great storyteller must have.

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.

items.title: Doce años sin Álex Angulo, el actor al que todo el mundo quiso
items.author: Gregorio Belinchón Yagüe
items.summary: Un documental recorre, a través de su hija, Dodó, y de los recuerdos de sus compañeros, la vida del intérprete de ‘El día de la bestia’, ‘Periodistas’ o ‘El laberinto del fauno’

images.caption: Lámina de El País Cultura

videos.caption: Video de El País Cultura

items.cleanReaderHtml: El 26 de julio de 2014, a las 17.30, un coche se salió en el kilómetro 114 de la AP-68 a la altura de Fuenmayor (La Rioja), en sentido Zaragoza. Dentro del vehículo solo viajaba su conductor, que probablemente se quedó dormido. Tras perder el control, el Audi chocó aparatosamente contra diversos elementos de la autopista. Cuando los bomberos accedieron a su interior, se supo la identidad del fallecido, Álex Angulo, 61 años, uno de los actores más queridos en España por el público y sus compañeros, un virtuoso estajanovista de la profesión que viajaba a Zaragoza al rodaje de la película Bendita calamidad. Más allá de sus filmes y de sus series, más allá de los amigos y de los fans, Angulo dejó atrás a su familia, y en especial a su esposa, Mayda Zabala, y a su hija Dodó, de 10 años: en el asiento trasero del coche estaba su alzador infantil. Doce años después, Dodó encara, apoyada por Zabala, una agridulce tarea: devolver los objetos que su padre atesoraba de sus compañeros, como recuerdo de grandes momentos, y charlar con ellos sobre su padre. El resultado es La maleta de Álex, un documental que se estrena este viernes en salas.

items.cleanReaderHtml: Al actor y director de cine Ethan Hawke (Texas, 56 años) le gustan el estoicismo filosófico y las Meditaciones del emperador Marco Aurelio. También siente pasión por las historias de aventuras tipo Jack London o incluso Rudyard Kipling, en las que el ser humano no hace frente a hordas de zombis o a un imperio galáctico. “Crecí viendo películas de acción que no trataban de efectos especiales, sino de personajes en situaciones extremas y realistas”, afirma por videollamada Hawke, el icono de, entre otras muchas otras películas, El club de los poetas muertos (1989) y la trilogía Antes de... (filmada entre 1995 y 2013).

items.title: The Third Thing: Poet Donald Hall on the Secret to Lasting Love
items.author: Maria Popova
items.summary: "Third things are essential to marriages, objects or practices or habits or arts or institutions or games or human beings that provide a site of joint rapture or contentment."

images.caption: Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Imagen extraída de la fuente original
The Marginalian

items.cleanReaderHtml:
“Third things are essential to marriages, objects or practices or habits or arts or institutions or games or human beings that provide a site of joint rapture or contentment.”

“The encounter between two differences is an event,” French philosopher Alain Badiou wrote in his tremendous treatise on why we fall and how we stay in love. “On the basis of this event, love can start and flourish. It is the first, absolutely essential point.”

And yet at the heart of this essential event is often something beyond the two — something often improbable, almost always inessential in itself, which somehow magnetizes the two differences into a unit of belonging.

The power of that mysterious and magical something is what the poet and essayist Donald Hall (September 20, 1928–June 23, 2018) explores in a gorgeous essay titled “The Third Thing,” which appeared on the pages of Poetry — the world’s most enduring and visionary poetry magazine — in the autumn of 2004.

Reflecting on his life with the love of his life — the poet Jane Kenyon, herself the keeper and giver of uncommonly clarifying wisdom on writing and life — Hall considers the secret to the kind of lasting love that blooms between the mundane and the magical. An epoch after Virginia Woolf exulted in “the bead of sensation” that punctuates the dailiness of any durational love to make it last, Hall writes:

Jane Kenyon and I were married for twenty-three years. For two decades we inhabited the double solitude of my family farmhouse in New Hampshire, writing poems, loving the countryside. She was forty-seven when she died. If anyone had asked us, “Which year was the best, of your lives together?” we could have agreed on an answer: “the one we remember least.” There were sorrowful years — the death of her father, my cancers, her depressions — and there were also years of adventure: a trip to China and Japan, two trips to India; years when my children married; years when the grandchildren were born; years of triumph as Jane began her public life in poetry: her first book, her first poem in the New Yorker. The best moment of our lives was one quiet repeated day of work in our house. Not everyone understood. Visitors, especially from New York, would spend a weekend with us and say as they left: “It’s really pretty here” (“in Vermont,” many added) “with your house, the pond, the hills, but … but … but … what do you do?”

What we did: we got up early in the morning. I brought Jane coffee in bed. She walked the dog as I started writing, then climbed the stairs to work at her own desk on her own poems. We had lunch. We lay down together. We rose and worked at secondary things. I read aloud to Jane; we played scoreless ping-pong; we read the mail; we worked again. We ate supper, talked, read books sitting across from each other in the living room, and went to sleep. If we were lucky the phone didn’t ring all day… Three hundred and thirty days a year we inhabited this old house and the same day’s adventurous routine.

What we did: love.

But the substance of this daily love, Hall argues, is not the stuff of romantic tropes. Echoing Little Prince author Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s beautiful insistence that “love does not consist of gazing at each other, but in looking outward together in the same direction,” Hall writes:

We did not spend our days gazing into each other’s eyes. We did that gazing when we made love or when one of us was in trouble, but most of the time our gazes met and entwined as they looked at a third thing. Third things are essential to marriages, objects or practices or habits or arts or institutions or games or human beings that provide a site of joint rapture or contentment. Each member of a couple is separate; the two come together in double attention. Lovemaking is not a third thing but two-in-one. John Keats can be a third thing, or the Boston Symphony Orchestra, or Dutch interiors, or Monopoly.

For Hall and Kenyon, the third thing was the pond near their home. He writes:

We had our summer afternoons at the pond, which for ten years made a third thing. After naps we loaded up books and blankets and walked across Route 4 and the old railroad to the steep slippery bank that led down to our private beach on Eagle Pond. Soft moss underfoot sent little red flowers up. Ghost birches leaned over water with wild strawberry plants growing under them. Over our heads white pines reared high, and oaks that warned us of summer’s end late in August by dropping green metallic acorns. Sometimes a mink scooted among ferns… Jane dozed in the sun as I sat in the shade reading and occasionally taking a note in a blank book. From time to time we swam and dried in the heat.

Hall’s most piercing point is that the third thing, rather than being an extraneous adornment of the relationship, is a central form of companionship. But while it is indispensable, it is not irreplaceable — it doesn’t so much matter what the thing is, only that it is.

When a landfill leakage destroyed their beloved pond, Hall and Kenyon still had their other third thing — poetry. Reflecting on its unparalleled power of perspective, its power to connect and console in the face of life’s darkest moments, he writes:

We lived in the house of poetry, which was also the house of love and grief; the house of solitude and art; the house of Jane’s depression and my cancers and Jane’s leukemia. When someone died whom we loved, we went back to the poets of grief and outrage, as far back as Gilgamesh; often I read aloud Henry King’s “The Exequy,” written in the seventeenth century after the death of his young wife. Poetry gives the griever not release from grief but companionship in grief. Poetry embodies the complexities of feeling at their most intense and entangled, and therefore offers (over centuries, or over no time at all) the company of tears. As I sat beside Jane in her pain and weakness I wrote about pain and weakness. Once in a hospital I noticed that the leaves were turning. I realized that I had not noticed that they had come to the trees. It was a year without seasons, a year without punctuation. I began to write “Without” to embody the sensations of lives under dreary, monotonous assault. After I had drafted it many times I read it aloud to Jane. “That’s it, Perkins,” she said. “You’ve got it. That’s it.” Even in this poem written at her mortal bedside there was companionship.

Hall’s 1999 poetry collection Without (public library) is the breathtakingly beautiful record of that abiding companionship. Complement it with Anna Dostoyevskaya on the secret to a happy marriage and Wendell Berry on what poetry teaches us about the secret of marriage and Adrienne Rich on honorable human relationships.

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.

items.title: Multas o imposibilidad de obtener un pasaporte: así funciona el voto obligatorio en el mundo
items.author: Jordi Rodríguez-Virgili, Profesor de Comunicación Política, Universidad de Navar
items.summary: Votar es un derecho, pero en algunos países también es un deber legal. La obligación dispara la participación, pero no garantiza elecciones libres ni ciudadanos más comprometidos.

images.caption: Imagen extraída de la fuente original
The Conversation

videos.caption: The Conversation

items.cleanReaderHtml:
El 29 de noviembre España celebra elecciones generales. Millones de ciudadanos acudirán a las urnas, pero muchos otros se quedarán en casa. En la mayoría de las democracias, votar constituye un derecho y los electores eligen a sus representantes o renuncian a hacerlo.

Otros países van más allá y consideran que votar es también una responsabilidad de los ciudadanos. Es lo que se conoce como sufragio obligatorio, y no se aplica igual en todas partes. Algunos países imponen multas y otros apenas castigan a quien se abstiene.

¿Votar es un derecho o un deber? La cuestión exige analizar los principios. Si el voto funciona como un derecho, la fórmula más coherente es el sufragio voluntario, que deja la decisión en manos de cada ciudadano. En cambio, si funciona como un deber, la norma que mejor encaja para obligar a participar es el sufragio obligatorio.

Si el voto es las dos cosas a la vez, entonces los principios no bastan para elegir y debemos atender a elementos como la participación, la legitimidad de los gobiernos o el coste que supone para quien vota.

De Chile a Brasil, pasando por Bélgica

La obligatoriedad suele aplicarse a las elecciones presidenciales, a las legislativas y a los referendos. Las elecciones primarias de los partidos, en cambio, casi nunca son obligatorias. Chile –que restableció el voto obligatorio a nivel general en 2022– y Uruguay mantienen las suyas como voluntarias. Argentina sí obligaba a votar en las PASO (Primarias Abiertas, Simultáneas y Obligatorias), pero las suspendió en 2025. Ahora el Senado debate suspender también las de 2027.

Las reglas cambian, además, según la edad. En Brasil, el voto es voluntario para los jóvenes de 16 y 17 años, los mayores de 70 y las personas analfabetas, y obligatorio para los demás. En Argentina, los jóvenes de 16 y 17 años pueden votar, pero la ley tampoco les obliga.

La exigencia puede variar incluso dentro de un mismo país. En Bélgica, por ejemplo, Flandes eliminó el voto obligatorio para las elecciones locales y provinciales de 2024, mientras que en el resto del país se mantuvo.

La obligación de votar consiste en acudir a las urnas, no en apoyar a un partido. En estos sistemas, el ciudadano puede depositar un voto en blanco o nulo.

¿Y qué sucede si un ciudadano decide no acudir a las urnas? Las sanciones oscilan entre una multa de 20 dólares australianos en Australia y la imposibilidad de obtener pasaporte u opositar en Brasil.

En otros países la obligación apenas tiene consecuencias. Bélgica contempla multas, pero no las aplica. En México, Costa Rica o Italia, el voto también se considera un deber, pero nadie es sancionado por quedarse en casa.

Los defensores del sufragio obligatorio suelen destacar tres ventajas. La primera es aumentar la participación. Si acudir a las urnas es una obligación, disminuye el número de ciudadanos que deciden abstenerse de forma voluntaria.

Chile ilustra bien este efecto. En 2012 adoptó el voto voluntario, y en las primeras elecciones municipales con ese sistema votó el 43 % del censo. En 2022, el Congreso aprobó recuperar la obligatoriedad, y en la segunda vuelta de las presidenciales, la participación subió del 56 % de 2021 al 85 % de 2025.

La segunda ventaja es entender el voto como una responsabilidad ciudadana. Como ocurre con otras obligaciones, participar en la elección de los representantes sería una forma de contribuir al funcionamiento de la sociedad.

La tercera es mejorar la representatividad. El politólogo Arend Lijphart sostiene en un artículo publicado en 1997 que cuando votar es voluntario, suelen abstenerse los grupos sociales con menos recursos, lo que reduce su peso en las decisiones públicas. La obligatoriedad pretende reducir esas diferencias.

La región de Flandes (Bélgica) emprendió el camino contrario a Chile. Al suprimir la obligatoriedad, la participación en sus elecciones municipales cayó del 93 % de 2018 al 64 % de 2024. Según un informe del Gobierno flamenco, dejaron de votar sobre todo los jóvenes, las personas de ingresos reducidos, las de origen extranjero y quienes tienen menos estudios.

El sufragio obligatorio también recibe críticas. Sus detractores consideran que limita la libertad individual y puede provocar que personas desinteresadas o desinformadas depositen una papeleta sin reflexionar sobre su elección. En la India, un tribunal frenó el voto obligatorio en las elecciones locales con el argumento de que el derecho a votar incluye también el derecho a no hacerlo.

¿Obligar a votar mejora la democracia?

El sufragio obligatorio no garantiza por sí solo una democracia de mayor calidad. Entre los países que lo exigen por ley hay varios que el instituto V-Dem, de la Universidad de Gotemburgo (Suecia), clasifica como autocracias electorales, esto es, países que celebran elecciones, pero no plenamente libres ni limpias. Es el caso de Turquía, Egipto, Tailandia o Singapur.

Una participación elevada no garantiza una democracia más sólida. Que casi toda la población acuda a votar no significa que existan alternativas políticas reales o que se respeten las libertades ciudadanas.

Tampoco existe prueba de que obligar a votar forme ciudadanos más comprometidos. Un estudio muestra que eliminar la obligación en Flandes provocó una fuerte caída de la participación en 2024, pero no alteró de forma significativa el interés por la política ni la satisfacción con la democracia.

España también conoció un período de sufragio obligatorio. La Ley Electoral de 1907 declaró que votar constituía un derecho y un deber legal para los varones que reunían los requisitos para ser electores. La medida se aplicó en las elecciones celebradas entre 1910 y 1923. Hoy, el artículo 23 de la Constitución española y la legislación electoral reconocen el derecho de los ciudadanos a participar en los asuntos públicos, pero no obligan a ejercerlo.

El debate, por tanto, sigue abierto. ¿Debe el Estado limitarse a garantizar que todos los ciudadanos puedan votar o puede exigirles que lo hagan? Al final, la pregunta va mucho más allá de quién tiene derecho a votar, incluyendo aspectos como hasta qué punto una democracia puede exigir a sus ciudadanos que participen en ella.

Las personas firmantes no son asalariadas, ni consultoras, ni poseen acciones, ni reciben financiación de ninguna compañía u organización que pueda obtener beneficio de este artículo, y han declarado carecer de vínculos relevantes más allá del cargo académico citado anteriormente.
